title: The Nishanwalia misl
hookLine: the standard-bearers of the Dal Khalsa

lines: DUST, NOISE, NO WAY TO SHOUT.
cards: Dust, noise, horses everywhere, and no radio, no phone, no way to shout loud enough. In a battle like that, how do so many riders know where their own side is? They look for the flag.
Whoever holds it up tells everyone else: we're still here, gather to this. Tradition says one band of the Khalsa had that job in the Dal Khalsa, and got its name from it. Today: the Nishanwalia misl.

teach.b: Three pieces. The word: nishan means a flag, a standard, a mark. Nishanwalia means the ones of the flag.
Not a village or a fort: a duty. The duty: tradition says that when the Dal Khalsa rode together, this band carried the Khalsa's standard, and its first chief, Dasaundha Singh, was its bearer.
Carrying the flag wasn't a ceremony.

teach.h: CARRIED WHERE IT COULD BE SEEN.
teach.b: The bearer rode where the fighting was, because the flag had to be seen. If it went down, riders lost their way.
So the bearer was guarded, and he guarded something bigger than his band: the sign that the Khalsa was still standing. In the way Sikh histories tell it, the Nishanwalias were not a large misl.
Their honor came from what they carried for everyone else. Then the flag you can still see.

teach.h: THE NISHAN SAHIB OVER THE GURDWARA.
teach.b: Outside gurdwaras flies the Nishan Sahib, a tall pole wrapped in cloth, with a saffron or deep blue flag bearing the Khalsa's emblem.
Sikhs say it marks a place where anyone can come in, eat in the langar and find shelter. Tradition traces the custom back to the Gurus' own time.
The Nishanwalias carried one in battle; Sikh communities raise one over their gurdwaras. Either way, the flag says the same thing: we're here, and you can find us.

how: Sikhs raise the Nishan Sahib outside gurdwaras and change its cloth with care at set times, and the Nishanwalia misl is remembered in Sikh histories as the Dal Khalsa's standard-bearers.

o: a battle cry shouted to rally the riders
a Sikh chief's seal on a letter
a flag or standard, a sign to gather to

p: the band's first chief and bearer

games.q: the Dal Khalsa is riding out. your band has been given the standard. the fighting is thickest at the front. where do you carry it?
o: at the back, where it's safe.
where the riders can see it, in the thick of it.
fold it away until the fight is over.
games.why: the flag had to be seen, so the bearer rode where the fighting was. if it went down, riders lost their way.

practice: Think of one thing you carry for other people: a family memory, a key to a building, remembering birthdays, the calm in a room when things go wrong. Let it come to mind and feel its weight and its worth.
On each breath, hold it a little more lightly without putting it down, and if you pray, let Waheguru go with the breath.

wordCard.voice: Nishan, a flag or standard, the duty that named the Nishanwalia misl, who carried the Dal Khalsa's standard so every rider could see where to gather. Today's word.

orig.note: Gurmukhi for nishan: a flag, a standard, a mark.

carryVoice: Your line: the flag-bearers. While the flag stood, so did the Khalsa. Day eight hundred ninety-five, done.
